Commandement der Zeemacht in het Caribisch Gebied

In November 2017, under the leadership of the MTC from Doorn, a three-week military tracking training was conducted. The objective of this training was to make the participating personnel skilled in tracking trails in the terrain. Additionally, they used military tracking with a realistic scenario in the training to also practice in a professional context. Six marines from 1-Troop participated in the training. These sailors were also deployed in various assistance requests in November to directly apply their new tracking specialty.

Training Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman

As part of the main task 'ready for deployment for territorial defense', the unit conducted an exercise in November in cooperation with the Joint Support Ship Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman. This collaboration enabled both the ship and the 32RSQN to practice amphibious operations. For 32RSQN, this was the first amphibious training aboard the Joint Support Ship. 1-Troop had a facilitating and training role during the exercise.

Military Assistance

In the autumn, the 32RSQN provided significant assistance at the request of the governor of Aruba with the following support.

Search Operation House (searching for weapons)

A mixed team of search-trained personnel and trackers (10 marines) searched a house in support of an investigation by the detective unit. The task was to find a weapon. The support ensured that the designated property was systematically, thoroughly, and quickly searched. Ultimately, no weapon was found, but the involvement of the search team minimized the burden on the local residents.

Search Operation

In November, 32RSQN, together with ARUMIL, supported the KPA in an urgent search. It concerned a missing person. It was presumed that this individual was a victim of a crime. The 32RSQN provided search capacity that made it possible to search more quickly across different axes. Ultimately, the person was found deceased by the KPA after further investigation.

Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean area focused on inventory management, particularly in the area of weapons and ammunition. The audit did not take place this year due to humanitarian deployment following Hurricane Irma in Sint Maarten. The KKW inspection revealed that a number of weapons were no longer permitted to be used. These were urgently replaced with new material. Additionally, a HACCP audit took place in the area of LDV. SAP MSKSAV increasingly relied on SAP and the corresponding Requests for Orders (ATB’s). As the barracks made more use of framework agreements, logistical processes became simpler and progressed more quickly. In 2017, MSKSAV also utilized a SAP consultant. This also led to an increase in the use of SAP. Staff received regular training, and SAP issues were resolved quickly. On December 7, MSKSAV was the first unit to go live with the SAP blanket orders, allowing contracts with suppliers to be processed more quickly and with less administrative burden. Preparations for the renovation of the company restaurant began this year at Zr.Ms. Zeeland at the quay in Sint Maarten.

Commandement of the Navy in the Caribbean

3rd Troop of the 32nd Reconnaissance Squadron (32RSQN) participated. As a result, the 13th Combat Command (CC) operated organically with three troops. The objective of the exercise was to operate with 'combined arms' in a live fire setting. For this, there was support from American tanks and anti-tank units, and from the Netherlands, the 15th Reconnaissance and Surveillance Troop (15e RSTA) and the 14th Combat Support (14e CS) participated in the exercise.

Emergency Aid to Sint Maarten, Saba, and Sint Eustatius

The 32RSQN, including ARUMIL, provided emergency aid in September on the Windward Islands after Hurricane Irma. The unit was already stationed on the islands prior to the passage. The 32RSQN was therefore the first unit to provide both hard and soft military assistance. The 32RSQN undertook the following tasks: staffing emergency shelters before and after the passage; supporting prison security; conducting patrols and setting up checkpoints at vital intersections; securing the air and sea ports to facilitate the transport of both personnel and equipment. Ultimately, the 32RSQN was active in the area for two weeks, after which the Maritime Support Task Unit (MSTU) relieved them.

French Commando Training in Martinique

It is an old tradition for units of the Royal Netherlands Navy Command Caribbean (CZMCARIB) to participate in French commando training in Martinique. This has been conducted in recent years under the name Unit Cohesion Training. The training maintains and strengthens the (strategic) partnership with the French armed forces in the Caribbean. Additionally, the participating units practiced: completing the French jungle training; validating personal physical and mental readiness; improving junior leadership at levels 2 and 3; validating the expeditionary mindset by operating in and under extreme conditions; and intensifying cooperation with the French headquarters in Martinique. The 3rd Troop, ARU, and CURMIL participated in the training. Prior to the start of the training, the 3rd Troop underwent an intensive preparation program and also completed the French and Dutch Jungle tests. The French commando training consists of three components: a jungle component, a maritime component, and the final exercise. Ultimately, 19 marines from the 3rd Troop and 10 ARUMIL participated.

Normally, military personnel attend the FLO conference in Beukbergen in the Netherlands, but not everyone was able to do so. Furthermore, a number of FLO participants reside in Curaçao. Therefore, this tailored conference for military personnel and their partners was offered locally. Landhuis Ascension is a place where people like to go for meetings, team-building sessions, or gatherings. It is also frequently used as a training location. Dutch and foreign units regularly set up a command post there in 2017 and transformed the parking lot and the immediate surroundings of the landhuis into a bivouac site with tents, trucks, and communication equipment. After the deployment of military personnel to Sint Maarten, debriefing meetings were held on Ascension to reflect on this special task together. In December, the traditional Christmas market took place, and a pleasant and well-catered veterans' dinner was organized.

Sint Maarten

The Royal Marechaussee has over 150 personnel working on various islands in the Caribbean. Therefore, the humanist counselor regularly travels to the Windward Islands and Bonaire to visit the personnel there. He can also be found at the Marechaussee brigade in Suffisant. 2017 will go down in history as the year when Irma ravaged Sint Maarten. Immediately after the storm, the chaplaincy was present on the island to assist affected military personnel and families. In September and October, many military personnel were deployed to Sint Maarten. The chaplaincy was also present for them, even providing stroopwafels during church services or reflection services. In Aruba and Curaçao, the evacuated families were supported, and the chaplaincy assisted colleagues with the intensive work.

Command of the Naval Force in the Caribbean Area Spiritual caregivers also participated in exercises. Exercises of the CIDW were faithfully attended, as well as those of CURMIL. The spiritual caregiver from Aruba participated in exercises such as the MOUT in the United States. On board Zr.Ms. Pelikaan, spiritual care was regularly present. Moreover, they frequently visited the various units; whether they were active at Parera or Suffisant, with the Coast Guard or with the brigade of the Marechaussee. In 2017, they participated in various events: Ride for the Roses, sports days, all hands, solidarity meals, barracks meetings, receptions, introduction days for newly assigned personnel, notification services, OPS briefings, Social-Medical Consultations, veterans' café, crisis interventions, KLM marathon, good causes committee, MSV, hospital visits at SEHOS, etc. Defense Materiel Organization/Joint Information Provision Command (DMO/JIVC) Team Leader: Lieutenant (ltz2) T. van der Wereld During the first half of the year, an inventory was conducted in preparation for the transfer of various ICT services (internet and telephony) from the CZSK organization to DMO/JIVC. In the second half of 2017, testing of the equipment to be used in the future began. A prerequisite for connecting the Marine detachment in Sint Maarten to the defense network was the dismantling of a microwave link and connecting the location to the fiber optic network of a local provider. This was accomplished in the third quarter of 2017. In the last quarter of the year, preparations began for adjusting the local passive infrastructure at MB Parera (fiber optic network) for the expansion of internet services and modernization of the WiFi internet network in the barracks accommodations.
Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean Divers are checking the seabed near Curaçao for explosives.

Command of the Navy in the Caribbean Medical Service CZMCARIB Head: Lieutenant Commander (kltz) C. Spaargaren Practice Manager: Lieutenant (ltz2) M.S. Boot In addition to primary care, the Medical Service provided operational support to local and external units at the Wacawa training area. This included shooting exercises, diving exercises, sniper training, camping, marches, climbing, cycling, and running. Additionally, training was conducted outside of Curaçao, such as HUREX, MOUT, and jungle training. In the first week of September, Hurricane Irma swept over the Leeward Islands. With a doctor and six Medical Assistants (AMV) on Sint Maarten, one AMV on Saba, one AMV on St Eustatius, one AMV on Zr.Ms. Pelikaan, and a medical advisor with a medical staff officer in Curaçao, a large deployment occurred. Furthermore, a trauma doctor, a staff doctor, a BME, and two evacuation teams along with a HPG member were flown in from the Netherlands to support and ultimately relieve the EGB personnel. Soldiers practice administering an intravenous line in Curaçao.
Attachments Zr.Ms. De Ruyter and Zr.Ms. Holland during SAIL.

Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean In April, exactly one year after the establishment of the EGB, the evaluation period ended and it was time to take stock. Despite the need for some minor adjustments, the EGB is performing well. By the end of the year, this had resulted in the awarding of a civil quality certificate (HKZ). The Medical Service is also innovating in operational areas. Following the deployment in Sint Maarten, it adapted its own emergency aid package. The materials that the Service needs during such a mission are now more flexible to deploy and better equipped for the type of assistance it must provide. The personnel are also enthusiastic about integrating with the operational units to improve collaboration and increase mutual awareness between both parties. Defense Security and Safety Organization (DBBO) Head: Mr. M.J.T. Hoek, from July 15 Mr. R.L. Bröker Access Control The department has adjusted the access control. In addition, it worked hard on the implementation regulations regarding the admission of suppliers. Patrol and Intervention DBBO conducted patrols and interventions together with the CUR and ARUMIL (blue platoon) to protect the interests of Defense. In addition to these main tasks, it also carried out the first response task, which is managed from the central control room at MBPAR. Training, Certification, and Education This year, the personnel received further training in their IBT skills to perform the above tasks even better. Various courses were also attended, such as APK II and APK III. Work Visits The following work visits took place from the Netherlands: C-DBBO together with C-BEV region West DBBO and SR P&O AIFB DBBO PM DBBO and Aost DV&B.

Attachments Working Visit of C-ZSK to the Corps of Cadets Almost annually, C-ZSK pays a working visit to the Corps of Cadets. These sessions typically take place informally in 't Zaaltje, the living room of the KIM. C-ZSK inquires about the well-being of the cadets, and the cadets question the flag officer on various topics. Annual Competitions From first-year to senior cadets, everyone participates. Because everyone strives for their year to come out on top. From volleyball to soccer. At the end of the day, the best always wins, and this is celebrated with cakes. Not too many, as the participants concluded the day with a dinner. Paresto provided the dinner in the company restaurant 't Oppertje. Working visit of C-ZSK to the Corps of Cadets.

KIM Cross - 50th Edition Under ideal weather conditions, the 50th edition of the KIM Cross took place on February 27. The start was at the soccer field of the Helder soccer club in Den Helder. Participants covered either 4 km or 8 km via paved paths, riding trails, and on the beach. For the cadets, participation was mandatory, but for many defense participants, it has become a baseline measurement for assessing their fitness level. Commemoration of the Battle of the Java Sea "All ships follow me!" Thus spoke Rear Admiral Karel Doorman. Near the bust of Doorman, in the garden of the KIM, the Battle of the Java Sea was also commemorated on February 27, which took place on that date in 1942 between an Allied task force under his command and the Imperial Japanese Navy under Rear Admiral Takeo Takagi. The Combined Striking Force of 14 Dutch, American, British, and Australian ships was defeated. The blow was particularly hard for the Royal Netherlands Navy (KM). In addition to Doorman, over 900 KM personnel lost their lives in the waters of Indonesia. KIM Cross 2017.

Great River Race In the first weekend of September, the Great River Race took place in London. Each year, a rowing team of cadets participates in this gigantic monster race. For approximately three hours, they row continuously along the River Thames. The results were commendable. This year, the team also finished in the top ranks. Ceremonial At various occasions, such as Prinsjesdag, the Commando transfer of the CZSK, Remembrance Day, etc., the CZSK organization calls upon the presence of (a delegation of) the Corps of Cadets multiple times. Installation Promotion 2017 In the presence of their parents, staff from the KIM and the FMW, and alumni from 50 years ago, around one hundred cadets were installed this year as well. Promotion 2017 began in early September at the KIM, after which they underwent the maritime introduction period at MKERF, Texel, and on board Zr.Ms. Rotterdam. The installation was the concluding event, after which they could return home for the first time. The Monday after the installation, the cadets departed for the Marines to the Van Ghent Barracks to follow the Practical Training to Officer of the Marines. The remaining cadets began their classes at the KIM. Assaut 2017 The Assaut is the gala ball of the Corps of Cadets, which is part of the cadets' curriculum. From start to finish, this celebration is organized by the cadets, and the KIM undergoes a true metamorphosis. This year's theme was: 'Once upon a time in the West'. Coast Guard Netherlands Captain (ktz) R.J. Blok MSc In 2017, the Coast Guard made several important decisions regarding the modernization of the organization as well as the manner in which it carried out regular Coast Guard tasks in the areas of service and enforcement. The (political) decision-making regarding the new MOC to be developed was completed on December 7 with the discussion of the letter to the House, formally launching the project.

Defense Simulation Symposium The second Defense Simulation Symposium took place this year at the ship handling simulator of the KIM. During the symposium, an interested audience listened to presentations from key players in the field, various workshops were held, and among others, cadets participated in demonstrations. Furthermore, there was ample opportunity to experience the latest maritime simulators firsthand. This year, the focus of the symposium was on maritime operations. The previous Defense Simulation Symposium highlighted land operations, and at a future event, the focus will be on air operations. The symposium was intended for all defense personnel involved in simulation systems as part of the Training and Education within the Readiness Process. Guest Lecture by the Royal Netherlands Marine Corps Band For the first time, the Marine Corps Band provided a guest lecture for the Corps of Cadets. "When is it appropriate to applaud? How do you know when a piece is finished?" By now, a large group of cadets knows the answers to these questions. The following evening, they were able to put their learning into practice in the presence of their parents. The Marine Corps Band held a concert at the theater de Kampanje for the entire Corps of Cadets, their parents, and the staff of the KIM. Dies Natalis (Birthday of the KIM) Annually, the KIM celebrates the anniversary (April 25, 1829) of the Institute. This year featured presentations by Captain (TD) ir. A.L. Vergroesen (MTPS, the technological master of the NLDA), Ing. C.A. Scheele (Astronomical navigation in Newton's spacetime - Past and present of astronomical navigation), and Dr. A.J. van der Wal (Astronomical navigation in Einstein's spacetime - Future of astronomical navigation). An interesting start to the morning included a solo musical interlude by one of the cadets on violin. Change of Command Commandant KIM Following the Dies Natalis, the Change of Command for the Commandant KIM took place. The now-promoted Commodore P. van den Berg handed over the flag of the Corps of Cadets to Captain (ktz) J.C. de Bruijn. SAIL Den Helder 2017 was the year of SAIL Den Helder, which also took place in and around the KIM grounds. The captains' dinner was held at the KIM, and the cadets participated in the crew parade.

Directorate of Personnel Foreword An NH90 drops off special forces from the Marine Corps during exercise Port Defender.

FOREWORD In your hands is the annual report of the Royal Netherlands Navy 2018. In this report, you can read about the deployments the Navy undertook during extensive international operations and exercises, as well as the actions taken by the shore organization to facilitate these deployments. The Navy once again made a significant impression during the Navy Days in Den Helder. Additionally, this year featured Velas Latinoamérica Curaçao, a unique celebration where several tall ships visited Willemstad. The Navy was also represented there. With many visitors, it was a great success and a wonderful opportunity to showcase what the Navy has to offer. The personnel underwent many new training programs and participated in (international) exercises. At the World Port Days in Rotterdam, the Navy was present with marines and ships to introduce visitors to the naval forces. We hope that this Yearbook will prove to be a useful reference work. Editorial Team Yearbooks Royal Netherlands Navy. Foreword by Commander (kltz) Rob Kramer, Commander of Naval Forces.

Royal Netherlands Navy Reserve The deployment of reservists has increased due to the introduction of the Adaptive Armed Forces. Career Guidance Career guidance explored future possibilities together with the employee based on personal wishes and what the organization had to offer in terms of positions. This exploration took place in the form of a career conversation that is held during each position, or once every three years. This conversation encompassed personal developments and wishes for the near future. This personal development of the employee was necessary to keep them valuable to the organization. In addition to internal mobility, the career counselor paid attention to external mobility for employees who will not progress in the long term but will leave Defense. The career guidance section consists of four military offices for the service groups, namely the operational service, marines, technical service, and logistics service, and an office for civilian personnel. At the beginning of the year, this section had 37 military and three civilian positions. Career guidance for civilian personnel had been in place for over a year. The evaluation of this new phenomenon is currently ongoing and will be completed in 2019.

In addition to the Dutch teams, teams from the United Kingdom, Czech Republic, Switzerland, Italy, France, Germany, and of course Poland also took part in the competition. A considerable international gathering with, as it turned out, many top shooters. This time, the competition took place at the outdoor range Biedrusko Military Training Ground near Poznan. The competition consists of seven events, where shooting is done with weapons supplied by and from the Polish army. Before a team begins shooting with a weapon, the procedures with the weapon are first practiced under the guidance of a Polish instructor. The instructor also assists the shooters at the shooting point. Although the Marine team achieved good results, they just missed out on the prizes. Fortunately, the KMR teams managed to win three awards; the second prize overall foreign team, the second prize overall individual, and the first prize for rifle. Sea Training Command (STC) Commander: Captain (ktz) A.S. Warnaar Last year, Commander Sea Training Command (C-STC) Captain (ktz) A.S. Warnaar was relieved on June 15 by Captain (ktz) R.W.J. Schoonen. Kuipers EMSD It was a special arrival in the Caribbean for the new SSCG Zr.Ms. Friesland. Among ten authentic tall ships and under the watch of thousands of spectators, the ship ceremonially entered the Annabaai as part of the maritime event Velas Latino America Curaçao (VLAC) on Sunday, July 15. Sinke Zr.Ms. Groningen was primarily focused on BO and training for most of the year. 5_KM_Annual_Report_2018_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-19 70 Operations Directorate Zr.Ms. Zeeland Commander: Lieutenant Commander (kltz) A. van der Kamp, from November 18 Lieutenant Commander (kltz) P. Bijleveld From November 18, 2018, to April 26, 2019, Zr.Ms. Zeeland was deployed as SSCG. Zr.Ms. Zeeland arrived in Curaçao in early December with a ceremonial entry. After a short logistical stop, Zr.Ms. Zeeland began executing its tasks. On the first patrol day, this immediately resulted in the interception of a transport with people without passports, who were handed over to the coast guard. In December, the ship facilitated the theme day of the Royal Netherlands Navy Command in the Caribbean (CZMCARIB). This theme day focused on the (simplified) military assistance requests and strengthening cooperation with local authorities in Curaçao. One of the three main tasks of Defense in the Caribbean is to support local and civil authorities. At the initiative of CZMCARIB, discussions were held on board regarding how and in what situations military assistance can be of added value. Additionally, the procedure for requesting certain assistance in Curaçao was simplified. This allowed for quicker action. The simplified assistance procedure applied to the deployment of military search, military tracking, diving operations, and static observations with binoculars and drones. With an attendance of nearly seventy partners from the security chain, including (representatives of) the government, Curaçao Police Corps (KPC), the public prosecutor's office (OM), Justice, Coast Guard, Royal Marechaussee, the Governor's cabinet, Customs, and representation from the Netherlands, the theme day was a success. As a result, a similar day will be organized next year for the chain partners in Aruba. During the port visit to Kralendijk in Bonaire, Zr.Ms. Zeeland, in the context of the 'Open Day of Defense', held an open ship together with Zr.Ms. Pelikaan. Here, the Army Company in the West (CidW), the Curaçao Militia (CURMIL), and the coast guard conducted various activities on the quay. Towards the end of the year, Zr.Ms. Zeeland intercepted a fast boat near Bonaire that was transporting a large illegal amount of cash. The naval ship also managed to disrupt a drug transport near the Windward Islands; during the interception action, the crew of a go-fast threw the contraband overboard to destroy evidence.

5_KM_Annual_Report_2018_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-39 90 Operations Directorate In February, the amphibious operations section was finally ready to publish its Maritime Doctrine Publication on Amphibious Operations. In March, the AR decided to continue the study on the Future Littoral Operating Concept (FLITOC). This process quickly became known as the 'roadmap mastering the littoral' (MTL). This was intended to lead to a complete revision of how operations from the sea are shaped. Given the small size of the MWC amphibious section, these activities are coordinated between MWC, S&A, and the group leader of the Marines. The roadmap describes a three-phase approach: from concept development, through force design to force development. This development is strongly coordinated with the United Kingdom and the United States, as they had recognized a similar need. This process is expected to take at least five years. After lengthy discussions, it was confirmed this year what had already been established in 2015 in a directive written by DGO. JKCMOX became the standard setter for Working at Height Cluster: “Operational climbing, descending, and moving on conditioned objects and in unconditioned environments using access, positioning, and fall protection techniques.” This meant that they determined what is safe and what is not for all climbing and descending techniques in an operational military context. This brought a whole stack of work with it, which meant that MWC was not in a hurry to carry out these activities on the bridge of Zr.Ms. Snellius.

Hydrographic Service Chief Hydrographer: Captain (ktz) M.C.J. van der Donck Offer Development Within IHO cooperation, new standards were developed for the unlocking of hydrographic data. This was based on S-100, the Universal Hydrographic Data Model. The transition to S-100 and the associated product specifications will commence in the coming years. It remains to be seen how the service will prepare for this and what the implications will be for processes, products, and services. The Hydrographic Service (HYD) decided to discontinue several products, including a paper chart of the Northern coastal area. A difficult decision was the termination of the innovative product Digipilot, which had been on the market for about ten years. As a legacy from the paper era, the Electronic Naval Charts (ENC) had long followed the layouts and naming conventions of the paper charts. However, the connection between paper and electronic charts is fading. Additionally, the organization of ENCs had become confusing due to changes in paper chart numbers and the combined use of 1800 charts and nautical charts. Therefore, a new, grid-oriented organization of the ENC portfolio will be implemented gradually. Demand Development The trend from paper to digital continued in 2018. The expectation is that next year the trend will level off due to the requirement to carry ENCs for SOLAS ships >500GT by July 2018.

New Parking Policy MBDH – First Wheel Clamp Placed at Naval Base Den Helder On Wednesday, October 10, the first wheel clamp was placed at the Naval Base. This new policy was established due to issues caused by illegal parking. This blocked emergency exits and access routes for emergency services. Directorate of Materiel Maintenance The review of the invoices for electricity, gas, and water has resulted in a record amount of identified errors totaling 5.7 million Euros for the year 2017. This amount would have been overpaid by the Ministry of Defence if the inaccuracies had not been discovered by the employees. A significant portion of the errors was found in the electricity annual accounts. The employees conducting the review, Ms. Wams and Ms. Ruiten, received a performance bonus for this, which was awarded on February 20, 2018, by Major General of Marines F.V. van Sprang and Captain (ktz) G.H. Nijenhuis. In April, the implementation of the first energy management system within the defence organizations of nine EU member states was completed. The implementation took a year and concluded with a visit from the auditors of the European Defence Agency (EDA) to the locations of the individual participants to conduct an audit. They also visited the Nieuwe Haven as the first defence location in the Netherlands with an energy management system. This pilot was led by Mr. R.J.L. Put from the EDB. The outcome of the audit of the Nieuwe Haven was positive, which means that the Ministry of Defence will implement this system at several major defence locations. In the KWS power plant, a replacement of part of the automation took place in May. The servers and programming setup were replaced, followed by an update of the software. To make the EDB more effective and prepare the organization for the future, after many consultation sessions, HMAROST on July 10 commissioned the organizational change, named EDB 2.0, to be implemented. In September and October, two compact transformer stations were installed, one at Erfprins for a temporary deployment and one at Maritime Airbase De Kooy for the new radar tower. Finally, in November, the 12kV main distributor in the KWS was extended with three additional fields. This allows the EDB to expand the 12kV network that the ships use, which is necessary given the increasing load from the ships.

Command of the Navy in the Caribbean 32nd Marine Squadron In line with the ambition to strengthen partnerships, the 32nd Marine Squadron (32 RSQN) invested in collaboration with local partner services in 2018. To ultimately become the relevant security partner in the region in general and Aruba in particular, further engagement was sought with the local disaster management staff; police, fire brigade, and coast guard. This collaboration led to various forms of deployment in 2018. With the simplified application procedure, several capabilities of the Royal Netherlands Navy Command (CZM-CARIB) were quickly deployable for the Caribbean islands within the Kingdom. As a result, the 32 RSQN was deployed several times for searching objects, tracking, and observing. Ultimately, the unit was deployed three times for static observation in support of the Public Prosecution Service and the coast guard. Additionally, it provided support three times for search operations in Curaçao and once in Aruba in support of the Public Prosecution Service. In 2018, the marines supported the coast guard in large-scale operations and specific assignments. Marines also assisted on the coast guard cutters in carrying out coast guard tasks. In 2018, the unit began providing a Guard Team for the station ship. This team can conduct boardings on vessels as part of anti-drug operations. The 32 RSQN was also on standby to carry out any emergency assistance operations, including humanitarian aid. As Tropical Storm Isaac approached, the units were moved to the Windward Islands in preparation for assistance after a possible destructive passage. A troop was moved to Curaçao and embarked on the station ship Caribbean Area, and a troop including squadron staff was flown in advance to Sint Maarten. The unit on this last island provided support to the local police. Due to the weakening of the storm, the unit on board the station ship was ultimately not deployed. In Aruba, the 32 RSQN provided support for the readiness of various safety services. The unit supported or organized various disaster exercises. For example, the unit participated in March in the exercise Carib Wave with different scenarios, ranging from a tsunami that had caused damage to the island to a tabletop exercise involving a bomb threat on board a cruise ship. For the runway overshoot exercise, the unit provided simulated casualties, simulating an aircraft accident. The unit also organized a hurricane exercise on the island, sharing experiences from Hurricane Irma in 2017.

Commandement der Zeemacht in het Caribisch Gebied The unit received and supported several units in Aruba during training and education. Together with the barracks, it provided support in 2018 for: A diving training from the United States Marine Corps; The military tracker (instructor) course; The Basic and Advanced training of the local militias; The training for frogmen; The training of the CidW of Curaçao; Ceremonial tasks during Dia di Bandera, Dia di Betico, King's Day, Remembrance Day, and the three arrivals of the station ship in Aruba; The events Highwinds (surf and wakeboard event) and the Aruba Regatta (sailing). In addition to deployment and support, the unit conducted various training sessions in 2018 to maintain or improve training and operational readiness. With the exercise Caribbean Urban Warrior at Camp Lejeune in the United States, the unit carried out its annual exchange with the American Marines in March. In this exercise, the unit was trained in operations in urban areas. The unique training location and opportunities at Camp Lejeune provide added value to the training level of the unit. In June, the unit underwent its annual preparations for the hurricane season. With the exercise in Aruba, the entire unit was deployed. Subsequently, the staff of the unit traveled to Sint Maarten for the hurricane exercise in the Windward Islands. Here, further agreements were made with the island authorities regarding support and military assistance in the event of a possible hurricane passage, together with the Marine detachment Sint Maarten. Due to the support during tropical storm Isaac, the annual tactical and dynamic shooting exercise in Curaçao could not be carried out. This was then adjusted and executed in Aruba. The tactical exercise was subsequently expanded in preparation for the exercise Tres Kolos. The emphasis was on cooperation with the French unit from Martinique. The two-week exercise was divided into a team competition and a tactical final exercise. After winning the team competition, the squadron began the tactical final scenario, in which the French and Dutch units had to carry out a simultaneous attack.

Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean has, over the past few years, made significant progress in addressing the backlog of national decisions (appointment decisions). In the autumn of 2017, HR Caribbean Personnel, in consultation with representatives from HRM Caribbean Personnel, ARUMIL, and the Departmento Recurso Humano of Aruba, developed a renewed flow policy for ARUMIL. This new policy has led to considerable improvements in the legal status of ARUMIL. A positive flow decision is now linked to the militia of ARUMIL when their initial employment contract is nearing its end. In practice, this positive flow decision was often associated with a decision to participate in the VVO (Voluntary Military Service). Upon completion of the VVO, militia members of ARUMIL were appointed as civil servants rather than as contract workers. This civil servant status provided a preferential position when the involved militia member transitioned to the Government of Aruba. By decision of March 6, this new policy was established by the Council of Ministers of Aruba. By decision of April 25, the Minister of Defense indicated that they would finance the accumulation of pensions and link it to the aforementioned positive flow decision. As of May 1, pension accumulation for this part of ARUMIL has become a reality. FRISC's from the Royal Netherlands Navy in Willemstad.

In 2018, a portion of all operational TRAs was completed. Due to issues with the availability of the renewed SharePoint environment, these TRAs could not yet be published. The system could not function properly due to the lack of central accessibility in the new SharePoint environment. Command of the Navy in the Caribbean From May 14 to 27, for the third time, a delegation from the Caribbean traveled to Lourdes. This delegation, coming from Aruba and Curaçao, joined the Dutch delegation, which thus consisted of 225 people. Together, they participated in the sixtieth International Military Lourdes Pilgrimage. Some flew for the first time, saw snow in the Pyrenees for the first time in their lives, but all gained an indescribable experience in the southern French location, where approximately 20,000 military personnel from 35 different countries met each other. Traditionally, the spiritual care organized the Christmas Eve celebration at MBPAR on December 24. In 2018, a Dutch task group departed from Den Helder to participate in the annual deployment NLMF Baltic Hunter 18 under the command of MBS. The Dutch task group consisted of Zr.Ms. Snellius, Zr.Ms. Makkum, and Zr.Ms. Vlaardingen. In addition to the combined training and exercises for operational readiness, the voyage also focused on the education and motivation of second-year cadets from the Naval Service Corps. After completing the basic theoretical naval training at the Royal Naval Institute (KIM), they were tasked with translating this into practical skills as naval officers on a naval ship. Last year, a group of 35 cadets participated in the deployment. After two weeks, a rotation took place to provide all aspiring naval officers with an equal practical experience. The emphasis was on safe navigation in busy shipping areas, accurate positioning, seamanship exercises, and participation in the large international exercise BALTOPS 18. The planned port visits provided the cadets with an opportunity to present themselves as good ambassadors of the Dutch Armed Forces during various courtesy visits. The sailing program of the six-week voyage took place in the North Sea, the Baltic Sea, and around the Danish islands. Installation of cadets.

POTOM The goal of the POTOM is that every student is capable of functioning as a Troop Commander of a Raiding Troop. The training had a logical progression in the responsibilities assigned to students, starting with small team drills and culminating in leading (complex) operations at the Troop level. The emphasis was on taking responsibility, learning to collaborate with fellow students and operational marines, managing stress, and developing tactical insight. A relatively large amount of attention was also given to the theoretical aspect of warfare for a practical training program. The guiding document for this was the British All Arms Tactical Aid Memoire (AAT-AM). From this document, the students issued their orders to their troops. This was standard in English to enable students to collaborate internationally with other countries such as the United Kingdom. The banner of the Corps of Cadets is the oldest banner of the Royal Netherlands Navy. In 1904, Queen Wilhelmina presented the banner to the Corps. This banner is unique in the Dutch armed forces as it is the only one that is not orange but red, as the cadets had a corps flag in those colors before 1904. During the May days of 1940, it was even brought to safety by some cadets and taken to Great Britain. Unfortunately, the banner cloth itself has been subject to wear and has been replaced over the years. Last year, the banner was also due for replacement. The applications on the cloth, the anchor, the royal crown, and the text have been embroidered using a 3D technique, giving it more relief. The worn cloth has been added to the collection of the naval museum.

An important national development was the upcoming large-scale construction of wind farms in the Dutch Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) under the energy agreement "Wind Energy at Sea." FOREWORD In your hands is the annual report of the Royal Netherlands Navy 2020. In this report, you can read about the deployments the navy undertook during extensive international operations and exercises, and the actions the shore organization took to facilitate these deployments. The year began as in previous years. This changed when, at the end of February and the beginning of March, COVID-19 also affected the Netherlands. Virtually the entire society came to a standstill, and the Royal Netherlands Navy had to adapt significantly. The lockdowns and safety regulations had a major impact on the workplace. The departments and units improvised and quickly regrouped so that the organization could function properly. In a safe manner, personnel followed many new courses, training sessions, and participated in (international) exercises. This was done differently than usual; sometimes from home, or in the workplace at a distance of one and a half meters. We hope that this Yearbook will prove to be a useful reference work. Editorial Team Yearbooks Royal Netherlands Navy. Foreword Commander of the Naval Forces Vice Admiral Rob Kramer.

Legal Affairs (JUZA) Head: Commander (cdr) G. Souer, LLD The JUZA department is part of the Directorate of Personnel and Operations (DP&O), one of the five line directorates of the CZSK. The department advises and supports the CZSK, the directors of the CZSK, and unit commanders on all legal issues that arise. JUZA provides legal advice and acts as a point of contact for the directors and commanders within the CZSK. Additionally, JUZA monitors the legal and administrative diligence of operations within the CZSK. The main areas of law that the department deals with include (military) criminal and disciplinary law, operational law, and constitutional and administrative law. These areas of law are organized into three different offices. Thus, every employee at JUZA can serve as the first point of contact (counter function) for questions directed to the department. JUZA does not provide legal advice to individual military personnel but does assist them if necessary. In criminal or disciplinary matters, JUZA is primarily involved on the side of the CZSK and the Ministry of Defence as an organization. Many organizational parts grew, either from the Van der Staaij motion or DOKM measures (temporary or not), as well as from strengthening the security chain. Furthermore, the measures from the Labor Conditions Agreement 18-20 were translated into regulations, from which HR measures followed. Part of this was the new Human Resources (HR) model developed by the Directorate of Personnel. The new model was intended to provide more opportunities for flexibility and customization for agreements between employees and supervisors. In fulfilling positions, the needs of the organization and the talents of employees in relation to the organization were better mapped and combined. New appointment and contract forms, strategic talent management, and the remuneration model are topics in the new HR model that affect the legal status of employees. A pilot environment at the Submarine Service has started to test some of these topics for feasibility. The Royal Netherlands Navy continued to face a significant personnel shortage this year. Measures to promote personnel retention were articulated in fourteen Personnel measures, drafted in September 2019 by the AR. The implementation of these measures received much attention alongside regular work. The measure to develop and implement a new HR system for CZSK was the most impactful. The old job allocation process was no longer functioning and needed to be simplified. To this end, a research study was conducted last year that will be further developed in 2021. It was investigated whether the Royal Fleet Auxiliary concept is applicable to a Hydrographic Survey Vessel (HOV), and the possibilities of 'alternative manning' for Combat Support Ships were mapped. The job vacancy bank was cleaned up to improve its functionality and transparency. Furthermore, it has been incorporated into operations that military personnel working at CZSK will be assessed once in their position. This could contribute to personnel retention, allowing for better alignment with the long-term objectives and development needs of military personnel. Royal Netherlands Navy Technical Training in Den Helder (KMTO) Commander: Lieutenant Commander (kltz) ir. M. Flaman EMSD The Royal Netherlands Navy Technical Training (KMTO) stands for "Inspiring". The motto of the Royal Netherlands Navy Technical Training (KMTO) is: "We train maritime technicians." The KMTO provides vocational and functional education for the personnel of the Technical Service (TD), but also for the (technical) personnel of other services and defense components. In addition, the school makes an important contribution to the training and development of crews of operational units, both above and below water. For training and development purposes, the KMTO has representative practical resources and simulators.

Students All new sailors and non-commissioned officers of the Technical Service (TD) of the Royal Netherlands Navy begin their careers at the KMTO. In 2020, 23 sailors started with the Entry-level Vocational Education (EVO) and 43 with the First Adjustment Module. Additionally, 26 non-commissioned officers, who already have operational experience as sailors, began their technical MBO 4 training in Service and Maintenance at the ROC Kop van Noord-Holland. Besides the 'regular' entrants, there are also VeVa students. The KMTO collaborates with ROC's spread throughout the country, which provide the VeVa training with a specialization in Mechatronics at levels 2 and 3. The VeVa students follow their vocational education at the ROC's and receive their Practical Vocational Training (BPV) at the KMTO. In 2020, 38 VeVa students started their BPV at the KMTO. In addition to the new intake, the KMTO provided the existing technical personnel with

By implementing measures such as reducing class sizes and allowing everyone who was not directly involved in teaching to work from home, (almost) all training could continue safely. Within the KMTO, the following three basic principles were applied: lessons that could take place remotely were conducted via distance learning; practical lessons that required in-person instruction took place on-site within the RIVM guidelines; and if compliance with the RIVM guidelines during in-person instruction was impossible, these lessons only took place after a task-risk analysis weighed the necessity against the risks. For all lessons requiring in-person instruction, procedures were established that outlined which specific measures applied to that particular lesson. To ensure that distance learning received the best possible support, the room was transformed into a virtual classroom. This allowed instructors to conduct distance learning while it felt as if they were in front of a normal class. Developments and Innovation The management of the KMTO noted that the intake of sailors had stagnated in recent years and that the market forecast indicated this was a structural trend. Additionally, the training pathway to sailor and corporal TD was experienced by the students as too long and too theoretical. To address these issues, the management of the KMTO developed a plan for the Technical Vocational School CZSK, which significantly restructured the training approach. An important change was that the education primarily took place at the workplace and that education at school was only provided when it could not be done (safely) on board or in the workshop. Since this change in education also affects the operations on board and the HR organization, it is being developed in conjunction and is a change that will take several years. In anticipation of the new structure of education and in response to the needs of the fleet, the vertical VVO was transformed from MBO3 Mechatronics to MBO 4 Service and Maintenance. For this, it was necessary to set up a revised VVO in collaboration with the ROC Kop van Noord-Holland. The experiences gained from this will be used in the Technical Vocational School CZSK. Due to COVID-19, it was impossible to continue the research with other institutions. An example of this was the joint research with the Katholieke Universiteit Leuven, Kortrijk department, and the Belgian Navy. Pul Head of Integrated Security Staff Office: Lieutenant Commander (kltz) P.B.A. Coster In 2012, the three-director model was introduced within Defense. This was the result of the defense-wide reorganization following the measures from the defense memorandum “Defense after the Credit Crisis, a Smaller Armed Forces in an Unstable World” (April 8, 2011). This reorganization was carried out based on pressing financial, personnel, and organizational frameworks. Based on this, it was decided at that time to divide staff, operational, and governance tasks of the Royal Netherlands Navy Command (CZSK) among the directors of Personnel and Operations and Material Maintenance, with the P-CZSK expected to fulfill the central coordinating role. In practice, it soon became clear that this organizational investment brought structural shortcomings in the areas of governance integrity, span/scope of control, allocation of responsibilities, oversight, and the absence of escalation levels. Furthermore, attention to personnel, operations, governance risks, and oversight increased significantly, and the intensity of governance coordination between internal and external interfaces grew. To achieve more balance in the governance organization of the CZSK, clarity in ownership, and in operations, C-ZSK requested the Chief of Defense Staff (CDS) to agree to the expansion of the framework of the three-director model. This provided the opportunity to establish a new directorate under a single leadership,

5_KM_Annual_Report_2020_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-36 95 The Operations Directorate's personal interaction and information exchange were significantly impacted by the pandemic. Restrictions on the number of personnel in the building and at the workplace, limits on the size and frequency of meetings, conferences, and working groups, and the closing of various international borders led to the necessity of quickly seeking alternative ways to remain effective. Fortunately, JIVC was able to rapidly roll out Skype and Ms-Teams for low classified virtual meetings, allowing everyone to increasingly communicate; in civilian attire from their kitchen tables. For the higher classified meetings, it was more complicated to get them off the ground. As a result, several valuable international contacts were at risk of being lost. The leadership of the MWC primarily focused on keeping the crew engaged with the organization, despite them being partially 'unwelcome' at the workplace. It was striking to see how the annually recurring meetings became increasingly limited in size and setting. Of the large meetings, the NATO Maritime Operations Working Group in Albania still took place more or less normally, but the Amphibious Operations Work Group was a virtual meeting. The Steering Group Meetings of the maritime COEs could take place in Ostend, Norfolk, and Kiel due to a temporary easing of the restrictions. However, various conferences, seminars, and working groups dwindled, were postponed, or were organized virtually (if possible). The Maritime Battle Lab remained very active despite all COVID restrictions and conducted activities for the MTMD forum, Spartan Windmill 3, Ship in the Loop test, Augmented Reality Tests, and Connectivity tests with the F-35. For the latter, the lab has recently acquired a mobile version of itself, which can be safely transported from Den Helder to any work location using Pelican cases (hard plastic cases).

7_Navy_Annual_Report_2020_COMMAND_OF_THE_NAVY_CARIB-1 124 Command of the Navy in the Caribbean Area Organizational Chart CZMCARIB.

the role of the Royal Netherlands Navy Command in the Caribbean region. The Command of the Navy in the Caribbean is responsible for maritime security, law enforcement, and disaster relief operations. The operational area is characterized by various factors such as the significant distance from the Netherlands, a large maritime accountability area, tropical climatic conditions, numerous direct political and international contacts, and culturally locally determined circumstances. 

Additionally, we observe three developments in the environment in which CZMCARIB operates that significantly influence our actions. Firstly, there is geopolitical destabilization in the region, particularly due to developments in Venezuela. A second development relates to the situation in Venezuela and concerns the increasing influence of criminal organizations. The country is in a humanitarian and economic crisis, resulting in an increase in migration of undocumented individuals and smuggling of contraband such as drugs and weapons. Finally, we see an increase in climatic extremes as a result of global warming. Whether CZMCARIB can adequately fulfill the three main defense tasks with its current capabilities is a legitimate question. In light of the above developments, the Advisory Council on International Affairs, at the request of the Minister of Foreign Affairs, is conducting a study on the role of the Royal Netherlands Navy Command in the Caribbean region.

6_KM_Annual_Report_2020_DIRECTORATE_MATERIAL_MAINTENANCE-21 122 Directorate of Material Maintenance Navigation and Training Bridge The Van Kinsbergen has, in addition to the regular navigation bridge, a fully equipped secondary training bridge. The ship is suitable for practicing all navigation procedures and safe mooring and unmooring. Deployment The Van Kinsbergen sails approximately 200 days per year. The main user is the KIM (Royal Netherlands Naval College). The ship is deployed to teach future naval officers (adelborsten) practical nautical skills necessary to work as a watch officer on the bridge of a naval vessel. The ship serves as a supplement to theoretical and (bridge) simulator lessons. Future navigation officers receive various training on board, such as mooring and unmooring. Additionally, the ship also has a formative function, including team building and character development. Besides the KIM, the Dutch-Belgian Operational School is also a major user. Students at the OPSCHOOL receive practical sailing training for the qualifications of non-commissioned officers for minehunters, hydrographic survey vessels, and submarines. Civil Maritime Schools The civil maritime school on Terschelling, the Maritime Institute Willem Barentsz (MIWB), also makes good use of the Van Kinsbergen for training future maritime officers. Within the framework of the agreement, the MIWB has access to the training vessel for several weeks. Second-year Maritime Officer students undertake short practical voyages on this ship. During their stay on board, navigation is particularly practiced. Additionally, the MIWB uses the ship for Advanced Fire Fighting training, where realistic emergency scenarios are practiced on board. Instructors from the MIWB provide lessons for the adelborsten of the KIM in Den Helder. These include subjects such as loading technology and maritime law. Within the framework of the agreement, there is an exploration of how to expand cooperation to further modernize and improve education within both institutions. Scientific Research Upon request, bridge teams from individual ships can use the Van Kinsbergen for tailored training or as part of a training trajectory. Occasionally, the ship is used for scientific research (TNO and universities) or for informational purposes.

Mission The mission of CZMCARIB is derived from the mission of CZSK and translates to the environment in the West as: "Providing security in the Caribbean." This one sentence articulates what CZMCARIB stands for and focuses at the strategic level on the realization of the three main tasks of defense in the Caribbean: Protecting the integrity and interests of the territory of Curaçao, Aruba, Sint Maarten, and the BES islands. CZMCARIB is responsible for the territorial integrity of the Caribbean countries of the Kingdom and Caribbean Netherlands. The own and visiting operational units have a so-called threshold function. Arrival of Zr.Ms. Karel Doorman in the port of Philipsburg, Sint Maarten.

Command of the Navy in the Caribbean Vision In order to realize the mission of CZMCARIB as adequately as possible in light of the changes around it, a vision has been established. The vision of CZMCARIB is: ‘CZMCARIB is the relevant maritime and security partner in the Caribbean, as part of the CZSK.’ This means that CZMCARIB aims to be recognized as the obvious and reliable partner when it comes to contributing to security in the Caribbean part of the Kingdom. ‘Relevant maritime’ and ‘security partner’ in the above vision refers to the fact that CZMCARIB assigns a high priority to the second and third core tasks. Due to national and international agreements, it wants to promote the international and local rule of law with its own resources, for example by contributing capabilities to (inter)national organizations or by providing military assistance. With these own resources, it can be deployed for a wide range of scenarios to support civil authorities, for instance for conducting searches, tracking, diving units, observation, and emergency assistance. CZMCARIB does this in good cooperation with national and international partners in the security chain. CZMCARIB also carries out the first core task. Through its forward presence, it fulfills a threshold function with its own personnel and resources. For an extended period, Zr.Ms. Groningen works together with the Royal Marechaussee during patrols off Aruba.

The Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean states that through our presence and our activities, we have a deterrent effect against potential hostilities from foreign countries or organizations. Promoting the international rule of law and stability is part of our second main task, which also includes the deployment for international law enforcement, such as combating the smuggling of weapons and drugs by sea. CZMCARIB promotes regional security and stability by, among other things, conducting counter illicit trafficking operations and through international military cooperation. The United States and France are the main international partners in this regard. C-ZMCARIB fulfills the CIT task as Commander Task Group 4.4 (CTG 4.4), a subordinate commander of the American Joint Interagency Task Force South. It supports civil authorities. The Dutch Armed Forces have developed into a structural security partner within the Kingdom. With its highly developed specialized and unique capabilities, the armed forces now have broader support options. CZMCARIB provides units that can be deployed for military assistance to Aruba, Curaçao, Sint Maarten, and the BES islands. CZMCARIB also provides support to third parties, primarily to the Coast Guard in the Caribbean (KWCARIB). C-ZMCARIB is also the Director of KWCARIB. It also provides emergency assistance in disasters and crises. Finally, CZMCARIB also supports the Social Development Programs in Curaçao and Aruba. 

International Drug Enforcement
In addition to the territorial defense of the six islands of the Kingdom of the Netherlands in the Caribbean, Defense plays an important role in upholding the international rule of law in the Caribbean. Given the location of the islands, this primarily involves combating international drug trafficking by sea. The navy in the Caribbean is closely integrated into the international drug enforcement organization Joint Interagency Task Force South based in Key West. The Commander of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean is therefore the commander of Task Group 4.4, one of the task groups of this organization.

As a result of the damage assessment, the ship returned to the Netherlands prematurely on January 1, 2021. In addition to counter-drug operations, the SSCG patrolled several times for KWCARIB in 2020, focusing on preventing refugee flows from Venezuela to the Leeward Islands. Counter-drugs All station ships patrolled for both the Coast Guard KWCARIB and CTG 4.4. Several successes were achieved. In cooperation with international units, CTG 4.4 and KWCARIB removed approximately 3,000 kg and 5,400 kg of contraband from the trade market in 2020 through seizures and the loss of clandestine cargo, respectively. This significantly increases the flexibility to quickly and effectively switch to CTG 4.4 during Coast Guard periods. Command of the Navy in the Caribbean Support Vessel Zr.Ms. Pelikaan Commander: Lt. D.M. Boom The year began for Zr.Ms. Pelikaan differently than any other year. The ship was not in Curaçao after more than ten years, but in the Netherlands for the Midlife Update (MLU). In the first months, everything went smoothly. The maintenance progressed steadily, and the crew regularly returned home to Curaçao in small groups to keep work and home life in balance. Unfortunately, starting in March, things changed from what was planned. Due to COVID-19, Curaçao went into lockdown. The crew that was in Curaçao could not return to the Netherlands and vice versa. Fortunately, the Netherlands did not go (completely) into lockdown, and all maintenance work on the ship could continue as planned. The crew worked hard on the renewed ship, and it paid off. What followed were the sailing material tests and seaworthiness tests. For the crew, it was mainly getting used to working with the newly installed much larger crane. After this, the signal was given to start the workup. With many new personnel, the learning curve for SARC 3 was steep, but the crew also overcame this hurdle. On September 17, Zr.Ms. Pelikaan departed towards the sea to Curaçao. The ship Zr.Ms. Pelikaan at the dock at Damen Shipyard for a Midlife Update.

Winnubst showcased its best side, and the hospitality of the KVMO and the KIM was also on display. With vocal support from Karen Klopstra and Marit Tesselaar and various musical soloists, the small hall of the KIM was more than filled. Then, in mid-March 2020, the cabinet announced the first general measures to combat COVID-19, and the Netherlands went into partial lockdown. At the KIM, the instructors sent the cadets home, and lessons took place online as much as possible. With the guidelines from the RIVM in mind, contact education could resume in early May, and after a quarantine period, sailing resumed with the training vessel MOV Van Kinsbergen and Zr.Ms. Urania. Nevertheless, in this exceptional pandemic year, it proved possible to welcome a group of approximately 100 aspiring cadets at the KIM. During the maritime introduction period (after the quarantine weeks), the future leaders learned how to act as team players within the armed forces in general and specifically within the KM. On Texel, the focus was on basic military training and pushing physical limits. This was followed by a sailing period aboard the Norwegian three-masted sailing ship Statsraad Lehmkuhl. Here, the aspiring cadets became acquainted with the sea and the elements. In addition, they learned how to safely perform seamanship tasks aboard a ship. The Maritime Introduction Period (MIP) formed the first part of the training curriculum at the KIM. This curriculum focused on competencies such as decisiveness, teamwork, communication, stress resilience, and sense of responsibility. Leadership is the common thread throughout the training. The aspirants are expected to ultimately be able to lead, guide, support, and delegate. This professional training is an essential part of the officer training program. Therefore, despite the ongoing pandemic, it was decided to carry out the MIP as fully as possible. To do this responsibly, the KIM implemented risk-mitigating measures, including a two-week quarantine period. The installation is an annual tradition, which unfortunately had to take place this year without the parents of the 2020 graduates and without the cadets from the 1970 graduation class who were installed 50 years ago (a drama for this graduation). 2_Navy_Annual_Report_2021_FOREWORD-in_memoriam-1 8 Personnel Directorate Foreword Divers in training in Den Helder.

FOREWORD In your hands, you have the annual report of the Royal Netherlands Navy 2021. In this report, you can read about the deployments the navy undertook during extensive international operations and exercises, as well as the actions taken by the shore organization to facilitate these deployments. The year began with COVID-19 measures, which caused many planned activities to be canceled. Nevertheless, the units managed to pick up the pace by creatively and responsibly resuming their work. Throughout the year, the measures were relaxed, allowing the Royal Netherlands Navy (KM) to deploy more extensively. In a safe manner, personnel followed many new courses, training sessions, and participated in (international) exercises. This was done differently than usual, sometimes from home or at the workplace while maintaining a distance of one and a half meters. After the devastating earthquake in Haiti, part of the island lay in ruins, and there were significant shortages of basic necessities. Various units of the KM set course for the affected island to provide assistance and deliver supplies. Marines were deployed to ensure that aid could be distributed safely among the population. We hope that this Yearbook will once again prove to be a useful reference work. Editorial Team Annual Reports Royal Netherlands Navy Foreword Commander of the Naval Forces Vice Admiral R.P. Tas took command on September 9 from Vice Admiral R.A. Kramer.
Zr.Ms. Holland off the coast of Haiti.

In 2021, COVID-19 had a significant impact on the operations of F&C C-ZSK. The vast majority of the work was conducted from home. During the General Political Debates, a motion from the VVD was adopted, providing an additional €300 million budget for Defense. This budget is intended to reduce maintenance backlogs in military equipment, barracks, other buildings, and ICT. For the Navy, this means an increase in the maintenance budget by €40 million structurally to reduce maintenance backlogs. Furthermore, at the end of 2021, the coalition agreement was presented, which includes a structural investment of €3 billion more in Defense. 3_Navy_Annual_Report_2021_ORGANIZATIONAL_OVERVIEWS-10 21 Organizational Overviews A marine during the annual Joint Arctic Training in Norway.

Organizational overviews years can take important steps towards both recovery and renewal of the organization. In 2021, in addition to the operational budget, the Defense Materiel Budget Fund (DMF) was used for the first time. The expenditures by CZSK were higher in 2021 than initially allocated at the beginning of the year. Compared to the draft budget, the Royal Netherlands Navy (KM) achieved more in readiness. Within material expenditures, the military component spent more in 2021 than indicated in the draft budget. The draft budget included a contribution to, among others, the Defense Materiel Organization (DMO) for the procurement of ammunition. This contribution was financed through the reallocation of personnel expenditures. Also, in personnel expenditures, KM spent a net million more in 2021 than indicated in the draft budget. The cause was the additional expenditures for hiring. The hiring included not only temporary workers but also the hiring of operational management and IT consultants. Evacuation Afghanistan On Monday afternoon, August 16, the operators of the Non-Foreseeable Special Operation section of C-Squadron were ordered to cut short their summer leave and report as soon as possible to the Nieuwe Haven in Den Helder. There, the entire equipment of the unit was packed and ready for action abroad. Upon arrival at the marsofterrein there, the marines learned that they would fly to Kabul together with two KCT teams and a BSB team to assist in the evacuation of Dutch citizens and status holders. Once landed at Kabul airport, the operators found themselves in a chaotic situation. Ultimately, the task unit facilitated approximately 2,500 people to safety via 21 Dutch evacuation flights, including more than thirty interpreters and their families. Directorate of Material Maintenance Naval Training Vessel Van Kinsbergen The MOV Van Kinsbergen is used for nautical practical training. Navigation and Training Bridge The Van Kinsbergen has, in addition to the regular navigation bridge, a fully equipped secondary training bridge. The ship is suitable for practicing all navigation procedures and safe mooring and unmooring. Deployment Annually, Van Kinsbergen sails approximately 200 days. The main user is the KIM (Royal Netherlands Naval College). The ship is deployed to teach future naval officers (adelborsten) practical nautical skills. These skills are necessary to work as a watch officer on the bridge of a naval ship. The ship serves as a supplement to theory and (bridge) simulator lessons. Thus, future navigation officers receive various training on board, such as mooring and unmooring. Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean is focused on countering drug trafficking by sea. CZMCARIB promotes regional security and stability by, among other things, conducting counter illicit trafficking operations and through international military cooperation. The United States and France are the main international partners in this effort. C-ZMCARIB fulfills the CIT task as Commander Task Group 4.4 (CTG 4.4), a subordinate commander of the American Joint Interagency Task Force South. The support of civil authorities is also a priority. The Dutch Armed Forces have developed into a structural security partner within the Kingdom. With its highly developed specialist and unique capabilities, the armed forces now offer broader support options. CZMCARIB provides units that can be deployed for military assistance to Aruba, Curaçao, Sint Maarten, and the BES islands. CZMCARIB also provides support to third parties, primarily to the Coast Guard in the Caribbean (KWCARIB). C-ZMCARIB is also the Director of KWCARIB. It also provides emergency assistance during disasters and crises. Finally, CZMCARIB supports the Social Development Programs in Curaçao and Aruba. Zr.Ms. Holland and a FRISC were deployed off the coast of Haiti.

121 Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean COMMAND OF THE NAVAL FORCES IN THE CARIBBEAN Staff of the Commander of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean, Director Coast Guard for the Kingdom of the Netherlands in the Caribbean and Commander Task Group 4.4: Brigadier (Briggenmarns) F.O. Borsje-Senders Mission The mission of CZMCARIB is derived from the mission of CZSK and translates to the environment in the West as follows: 'Providing security in the Caribbean.' This one sentence encapsulates what CZMCARIB stands for and focuses at the strategic level on the realization of the three main tasks of defense in the Caribbean: Protecting the integrity and interests of the territory of Curaçao, Aruba, Sint Maarten, and the BES islands. CZMCARIB is responsible for the territorial integrity of the Caribbean countries of the Kingdom and Caribbean Netherlands. The own and visiting operational units have a so-called threshold function. This means that through our presence and our activities, we have a deterrent effect against potential hostilities from foreign countries or organizations. Promoting the international rule of law and stability. The second main task also includes the deployment for international law enforcement, such as combating the smuggling of weapons and

Command of the Navy in the Caribbean Area Vision In order to realize the mission of CZMCARIB as adequately as possible in light of the surrounding changes, a vision has been established. The vision of CZMCARIB is: ‘CZMCARIB is the relevant maritime and security partner in the Caribbean, as part of the CZSK’. This means that CZMCARIB aims to be recognized as the obvious and reliable partner when it comes to contributing to security in the Caribbean part of the Kingdom. ‘Relevant maritime’ and ‘security partner’ in the above vision refers to the fact that CZMCARIB assigns a high priority to the second and third core tasks. Due to national and international agreements, it wants to promote the international and local rule of law with its own resources, for example by contributing capabilities to (inter)national organizations or by providing military assistance. With these own resources, it can be deployed for many diverse scenarios to support civil authorities, for example for conducting searches, tracking, diving units, observation, and emergency assistance. CZMCARIB does this in good cooperation with national and international partners in the security chain. Reflection on 2021 Just like in 2020, COVID-19 also dominated this year. The pandemic had a significant impact on the operations of CZMCARIB as well as its operational activities. Local authorities, particularly from Curaçao, regularly called upon military assistance to support them with COVID-19 related activities. International Drug Enforcement In addition to the external defense of six islands of the Kingdom of the Netherlands in the Caribbean, the Defense plays an important role in maintaining the international rule of law in the Caribbean area. Given the location of the islands, this primarily involves combating international drug trafficking by sea. The Navy in the Caribbean is thus closely integrated into the international drug enforcement organization Joint Interagency Task Force South based in Key West. The Commander (kltz) of the Navy in the Caribbean is therefore the commander of Task Group 4.4, one of the task groups of this organization.

Command of the Navy in the Caribbean The task assigned to CZMCARIB from the Land Packages is to professionalize the Caribbean military, including modernizing the legal position and (re)establishing the Social Development Program for disadvantaged youth in both Aruba and Curaçao. Throughout the year, the department began drafting the CZMCARIB Ambition Document. This document looks ten years ahead and describes both the ambition in terms of personnel and equipment. The goal is to complete the Ambition Document in 2022 and formally present it to C-ZSK. Despite COVID-19, CMCARIB made a strong effort to expand the CARIB training hub. For example, work was done on a Forward Operating Base at the Wacawa training area in Curaçao and on a training village for Urban Operations at the Marine Barracks Savaneta in Aruba. In 2021, CZMCARIB took the first steps to pay extra attention to real estate in the area. The state of maintenance is insufficient, office spaces and barracks often do not meet standards, and various installations are no longer maintainable, including air handling systems. Relief goods are being unloaded in Haiti.

In collaboration with international units, approximately 10,200 kg and 1,900 kg of contraband were removed from the trade market in 2021 by CTG 4.4 and KWCARIB, respectively, through confiscation. These international operations were carried out by the ship with various countries such as the United States, France, Colombia, and the United Kingdom. Hurricane Relief Assistance Where in 2020 COVID-19 disrupted plans, the Hurricane Relief Exercise (HUREX) took place in 2021 in preparation for the hurricane season. From May 26 to June 5, rehearsals were conducted in the Windward Islands for the hurricane season, which runs from June 1 to November 30. During the exercise, MHKC worked closely with local authorities and aid organizations to ensure smooth cooperation during the hurricane season. As a result, an NH90 flies over the affected Haiti.

In 2021, the Control Department of CZMCARIB worked to support C-ZMCARIB in the preparation, execution, progress, and quality of financial policy advice. It also compiled the budget, established the spending program, and provided management and steering reports. 

Finance: In 2021, CZSK made budget cuts in several areas. In this process, less budget was allocated to the Caribbean than was originally available. CZMCARIB had a budget of 18.7 million euros in 2021. Due to limited travel opportunities caused by the COVID-19 pandemic and the fact that fewer external units conducted exercises in the Caribbean, fewer activities took place. CZMBARIB also organized fewer activities for its own units due to the pandemic. As a result, most foreign exercises were canceled, and units traveled much less between the islands for training. The realization of the budget fell short as a result. Furthermore, the establishment of the Country Package led to a 12.5% reduction in the salaries of local staff. The Social Development Programs were not executed, and the additional personnel capacity within the development of Caribbean Military Personnel (CARMIL) was not filled immediately. Because CZMCARIB paid the currency claim of 1.9 million euros itself, the full budget was realized in 2021.

Management Information: In 2021, CZMCARIB reported on the year 2020 based on a plan-do-check-act cycle and prepared the annual plan for 2022. With this annual plan, they looked not only at the short term but also at the long term to be able to plan in a timely manner. In further improving operations, the focus was on enhancing the quality of input and securing the changed operations, with the motto 'strong together.'

Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean opened the CURMIL to women, which had not been possible before. Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean in 2021 was also dominated by the concerns of the pandemic. The EGB provided personnel to the local GGD after a previous support request to assist in GGD COVID-19 testing sites, conducting contact tracing among its own ranks, and opening its own testing site at MBPAR. The organization also provided daily care for positively tested personnel who were placed in quarantine at MKSUF. This continued throughout the year. In addition to this care, a vaccination program was initiated in Curaçao by the local GGD. On April 1, they requested EGB to assist them by opening a site at MBPAR to administer vaccinations to military personnel and their family members, as well as to civil servants in crucial professions from the country and kingdom. On April 4, EGB military personnel vaccinated at MBPAR, and the medical teams from CIDW and a local nurse from the Curaçao militia also administered shots. On the opening day, they provided vaccinations to over 1,000 people (well above the numbers at other vaccination sites on the island). Therefore, this continued for another two and a half weeks at the base. After this period, this site was closed, and EGB supported other vaccination centers in the country with personnel. In addition to all pandemic-related care, the service supported military training and exercises that continued throughout the year. Vaccination of military personnel.
