Goetzee The main tasks that BMW performs in the Caribbean region are assistance, service provision, reporting, support after traumatic events, and crisis intervention. For the CARIB region, the service, together with the Chaplaincy Service and in Aruba also with P&O, is responsible for notifying family announcements. They are available on a 24/7 basis for personnel and their families. This was the second year in which COVID-19 played a restrictive role, but the situation normalized during 2021, allowing for more regular opportunities to carry out the work. For instance, the service resumed work visits to Bonaire, where the KMar is active, and to Sint Maarten to be more accessible to personnel and their families on these islands. After the emergency aid to Haiti, the department provided aftercare for the units that were deployed. In addition to the regular BMW support for employees and their families, activities for post-active veterans resumed in 2021. In Curaçao, the Veterans Association Curaçao was active and represents the interests of veterans residing on the island. BMW was in contact with this association to provide access for veterans living in Curaçao and Aruba from the position as a partner within the National Care System for Veterans. On both islands, various assistance contacts with post-active veterans were established. As part of veteran care, the service also maintained contact with the Veterans Care Desk of the General Civil Pension Fund in the Netherlands. Medical Service CZMCARIB Head: Captain (ktz) R.J. The way in which the partners collaborated with the Coast Guard to carry out their tasks as effectively as possible despite these measures proved to be a reliable and stable factor in 2021. The flexibility of personnel and resources was crucial in this regard. The task of maritime security is taking more shape within the Coast Guard, and starting this year, a separate chapter has been dedicated to the implementation of this new, third main task in the Annual Report. For the proper execution of particularly pre-arrival analyses, the right resources were not yet made available to the Coast Guard in 2021. In addition to regular Coast Guard tasks, a Coast Guard aircraft was deployed during two periods in the context of EU-Frontex in the Mediterranean Sea, as well as during the flooding in Limburg. The aircraft of the Coast Guard flew a record number of flight hours in 2021, and the agreements regarding the deployment of SAR helicopters have been improved. Due to the withdrawal of vessels from the Rijksrederij of more than twenty percent, the deployment of these vessels at sea fell short of the assignment from the Combined Annual Plan. The renewal and modernization of the Coast Guard is taking more shape. Not only has progress been made in the ICT part of the Maritime Operations Center project, but in 2021, the architect and project management were selected for the new construction, an important step towards the realization of the new operations center. Intensive work has been done with the commissioning parties of the Coast Guard and the Rijksrederij to find a solution for the implementation of the 24/7 enforcement concept with the existing vessels. An important development in the tasks of the Coast Guard is the intensification of tasks to ensure shipping safety in the context of offshore wind energy. The ongoing construction of wind farms in the North Sea requires additional monitoring of shipping. To this end, an extra desk has been set up at the CCC, additional personnel have been recruited, and since 2021, one additional Emergency Recovery & Towing Vessel has been patrolling in the southern North Sea. For the influx of personnel, a limited reorganization process was completed in 2021. Progress has been made in the development of the internal organization of the Coast Guard due to the influx of new personnel in previous years, both in operational and supporting processes. This is particularly visible in the crisis organization, structuring functional ICT management, implementing GDPR legislation, documenting processes, and renewing operational agreements with partner services.

Directorate of Personnel Foreword The 76 mm gun of Zr.Ms. Van Amstel in action during an exercise.

FOREWORD In your hands, you have the Yearbook of the Royal Netherlands Navy 2022. In this, you can read about the deployments the navy undertook during extensive international operations and exercises, as well as the actions taken by the shore organization to facilitate these deployments. Although some COVID-19 measures were still in place at the beginning of the year, the government gradually lifted these restrictions, allowing for more activities. Thus, exercises and events could continue, and normalcy returned. The Royal Netherlands Navy (KM) once again made a significant impression during the Navy Days in Den Helder. Additionally, this year saw Velas Latinoamérica Curaçao, a unique celebration featuring several tall ships visiting Willemstad. The KM was also represented there. With many visitors, it was a great success and a wonderful opportunity to showcase what the KM has to offer. The personnel underwent many new trainings, courses, and participated in (international) exercises. At the World Port Days in Rotterdam, the navy was present with marines and ships to introduce visitors to the naval forces. We hope that this Yearbook will once again prove to be a useful reference work. Editorial Team Yearbooks Royal Netherlands Navy Foreword Commander of Naval Forces Vice Admiral R.P. Tas.

Organizational Overviews In 2022, CZSK (Royal Netherlands Navy Command) spent a net € 101 million more on personnel expenses than was included in the draft budget. The cause of this is primarily due to additional expenses resulting from the collective labor agreement 2021-2023, temporary salary structure allowances, and increased compensation for pension costs. Due to underfilling of permanent staff, expenditures for hiring temporary workers and consultants for operational management and IT were higher than anticipated. This hiring was necessary to procure essential personnel in order to prevent stagnation in the execution of the Navy's tasks as much as possible. In 2022, CZSK received € 3.3 million more in the operational budget than was included in the draft budget. This was mainly caused by a higher contribution from the countries to the Caribbean Coast Guard (catching up on backlog) from previous years. Defense Materiel Fund (DMF) In the DMF, expenditures in 2022 were higher than the budget allocated at the beginning of the year (€ 155 million) plus additional allocations (€ 97 million). However, due to a budget (€ 83 million) being deferred to 2026 through a cash shift, a surplus of € 33 million was presented as of December 31. This is mainly due to a higher reliability of delivery of goods and services than was estimated at the time of the cash shift, resulting in more being realized. The budget shifted to 2026 can be used to cover potential future shortfalls in the DMF. Additionally, within the fund in 2022, € 13.4 million more was received due to extra efforts in collecting overdue invoices. This includes CZSK catching up from previous years (e.g., maintenance on Portuguese M-frigates) and, in net terms, higher incidental VAT receipts. These extra receipts are and will be used for the maintenance of maritime materiel.

Schelkers The JUZA department is part of the Directorate Personnel and Organization (DP&O), one of the four line directorates of CZSK. The department advises and supports CZSK, the directors of CZSK, and commanders of units on all legal issues that arise. JUZA provides legal advice and acts as a point of contact for the directors and commanders within CZSK. Additionally, JUZA monitors the legal and administrative diligence of operations within CZSK. The main areas of law that the department deals with include (military) criminal and disciplinary law, operational law, and state and administrative law. These areas of law are organized into three different offices. Thus, every employee at JUZA can serve as the first point of contact (counter function) for questions directed to the department. JUZA does not provide legal advice to individual military personnel but does assist them if necessary. In criminal or disciplinary matters, JUZA is primarily involved on the side of CZSK and Defense as an organization. If a military member is involved in a criminal case, they can receive assistance from Defense in that matter.

The school bid farewell to the partially overlapping five intake moments and transitioned to four intakes per year. Intake 1 was the last group to experience the drastic COVID-19 measures. SMVBO divided the group in such a way that half started two weeks later and ultimately swore them in together with intake 2. This also marked the start of this ceremony at the Kampanje location. To reduce early and possibly unnecessary dropouts, the school adjusted the structure of the EMMV and introduced "the soft landing." As part of this, SMVBO developed the Pre-Intake. In this program, students undergo a three-day program four to six weeks before the intake date, during which a baseline measurement for the Physical Fitness Test and swimming is taken, and a fitting moment at the KPU allows the student to break in their combat boots and better prepare physically. Additionally, the school changed the structure of the EMMV by no longer going directly to Texel for the relatively demanding bivouac program for untrained students. It involved a more balanced buildup in the number of marching kilometers and the weight of the carried equipment. From now on, an introductory bivouac of three days will be conducted at Marine Barracks Erfprins, followed by a mid-bivouac of five days on Texel, and concluding with the Volharding, which has been extended from two to three days. The program has also been adjusted to "lead" the students in the first two weeks, then "guide" them for two weeks, and finally work them up towards the Volharding by "supporting" them. Pul Head of Integrated Security Staff Office: Lieutenant Commander (kltz) (SD) J. van Rijn In November 2019, the Directorate of Integrated Operations & Governance (IB&B) was established. The aim of this consolidation of departments focused on operations and governance within the CZSK was: to achieve greater integration and effectiveness in operations and governance; to provide improved management of the safety organization; to realize a better distribution of the workload within the various directorates of CZSK. From December 2020 to March 2021, the directorate conducted an evaluation. One of the conclusions was that the above objectives had not been fully achieved. This has various causes. At the establishment of the directorate, it was based on the existing structures. At that time, no organizational improvements were made other than an administrative reorganization. The intended synergy between the different departments was not yet fully achieved through this reorganization. Additionally, the Governance Staff initiated various developments in recent years that directly impacted the organization of the IB&B directorate. This includes the establishment of the CIO system, the embedding of Portfolio and Program Management (P3O), the strengthening of short-cycle innovation, and the strengthening of Safety and Environment (V&M). As a result of the introduction of the new top structure within Defense, the interfaces between the directorate and the Governance Staff also changed. For effective realization of the objectives, it was necessary to logically cluster the tasks. This clustering had to align with BBD2020 and DN 2022.

5_KM_Annual_Report_2022_OPERATIONS_DIRECTORATE-38 99 Operations Directorate Maritime Warfare Centre (MWC) Head: Colonel (ltkolmarns) J. de Wolf The year 2022 was primarily focused on rebalancing for the MWC, restoring balance after the pandemic. This involved restructuring part of the capacity to better meet the demands of the Royal Netherlands Navy Command (CZSK). It led to the establishment of a Subject Matter Expert (SME) for Maritime Unmanned & Autonomous Systems, the creation of an additional SME for Anti-Submarine Warfare (VTE filled after four years of vacancy), and the merging of capabilities for Maritime Ballistic Missile Defence and Above Water Warfare. This did come at the expense of the VTE SME Operational Technology, which means that CZSK must draw on expertise elsewhere for the Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear dossier. Driven by personnel shortages, the centre must apply a more forced and sharper delineation of tasks. The MWC's core task is to support the Force Development of the operational navy broadly, developing the contemporary navy into the navy of tomorrow. The focus is on practical support at a low-tactical level with a conceptual approach. Strategic issues are primarily addressed in The Hague and at S&A, while hard technology development is mainly the responsibility of the Defence Materiel Organization (DMO), with the understanding that the MWC remains in continuous consultation with the aforementioned departments. However, the centre also continues to work on a strong network of knowledge partners. The rebalancing here mainly involves re-establishing contacts that were lost during COVID-19. The external pressure on the MWC as a knowledge provider increased significantly this year. Due to the growing tensions in the world, the Defence budget steadily rose, creating more opportunities for new projects, as well as expansion, re-evaluation, and/or acceleration of ongoing investment projects. Wherever maritime capacity review was concerned, Defence called upon the MWC to provide capacity and expertise to support planning. At the same time, more regular (inter)national meetings could again be organized physically. This was done extensively to restore ties between various knowledge parties. A summary of the key meetings: From March 8 to 10, the Head of Maritime Battle Lab (H-MBL) participated in the User Group Meeting for Evolved SeaSparrow Missile Block 1 and 2 at the Naval Air Warfare Center China Lake in the United States.

Directorate of Material Maintenance Deployment Each year, Zr.Ms. Van Kinsbergen sails for approximately 200 days. The main user is the Royal Netherlands Naval College (KIM). The ship is deployed to teach future naval officers (adelborsten) practical nautical skills. These skills are necessary to work as a watch officer on the bridge of a naval vessel. The vessel serves as a supplement to theory and (bridge) simulator lessons. Future navigation officers receive various training on board, such as mooring and unmooring. Additionally, the ship also has a formative function, including team building and character development. Besides the KIM, the Dutch-Belgian Operational School is also a major user. Students at the OPSCHOOL receive practical sailing training for the qualifications of non-commissioned officers for minehunters, hydrographic survey vessels, and submarines. Civil Maritime Schools The civil maritime school on Terschelling, the Maritime Institute Willem Barentsz (MIWB), also makes good use of Zr.Ms. Van Kinsbergen for training future maritime officers. Within the framework of the agreement, the MIWB has access to the training vessel for several weeks. Second-year Maritime Officer students undertake short practical trips on this ship. During their stay on board, navigation is particularly practiced. Additionally, the MIWB uses the ship for Advanced Fire Fighting training, where realistic emergency scenarios are practiced on board. Instructors from the MIWB provide lessons for the adelborsten of the KIM in Den Helder. These lessons cover subjects such as loading technology and maritime law. Within the agreement, there is an exploration of how to expand cooperation to further modernize and improve education within both institutions. Scientific Research Upon request, bridge teams from individual ships can use Zr.Ms. Van Kinsbergen for tailored training or as part of a training program. Occasionally, the ship is used for scientific research (TNO and universities) or for informational purposes. Two Crews Zr.Ms. Van Kinsbergen has two crews of five persons each; a military and a civilian crew. The latter consists of a captain, a first and a second mate, a chief engineer, and a cook. The military crew consists of a commander (kltz), a senior officer, a skipper with sailing qualifications, a chief technical officer, and a cook.

Philipse-Breitenstein Mission The mission of CZMCARIB is derived from the mission of CZSK and translates to the environment in the West as: 'Providing security in the Caribbean.' This one sentence articulates what CZMCARIB stands for and focuses at the strategic level on the realization of the three main tasks of defense in the Caribbean: Protecting the integrity and interests of the territory of Curaçao, Aruba, Sint Maarten, and the BES islands. CZMCARIB is responsible for the territorial integrity of the Caribbean countries of the Kingdom and Caribbean Netherlands. The own and visiting operational units have a so-called threshold function. This means that through our presence and our activities, we have a deterrent effect against potential hostilities from foreign countries or organizations. Promoting the international rule of law and stability. The second main task also includes deployment for international law enforcement, such as combating the smuggling of weapons and drugs by sea. CZMCARIB promotes regional security and stability by, among other things, carrying out

CZMCARIB provides units that can be deployed for military assistance to Aruba, Curaçao, Sint Maarten, and the BES islands. CZMCARIB also provides support to third parties, primarily to the Coast Guard in the Caribbean (KWCARIB). C-ZMCARIB is also the Director of KWCARIB. It also provides emergency aid during disasters and crises. Finally, CZMCARIB also supports the Social Development Programs in Curaçao and Aruba. Vision To realize the mission of CZMCARIB as adequately as possible in light of the surrounding changes, a vision has been established. The vision of CZMCARIB is: ‘CZMCARIB is the relevant maritime and security partner in the Caribbean, as part of the CZSK.’ Arrival of Zr.Ms. Friesland in Willemstad.

Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean This means that CZMCARIB aims to be recognized as the obvious and reliable partner when it comes to contributing to security in the Caribbean part of the Kingdom. 'Relevant maritime' and 'security partner' in the above vision refers to the fact that CZMCARIB assigns a high priority to the second and third primary tasks. Due to national and international agreements, it aims to promote the international and local rule of law with its own resources, for example by contributing capabilities to (inter)national organizations or by providing military assistance. Reflection on 2022 With the global decline of the pandemic, activities in the CARIB (both military and civilian) gradually gained momentum. The number of training activities in the CARIB as a training hub increased throughout the year, as did the participation of its own units in exercises elsewhere in the region. This provided a positive boost to operational readiness. On February 24, Russia invaded Ukraine. Just as in the Netherlands, the Alert State was raised in the West, a situation that was maintained throughout the year. Additionally, in mid-2022, Velas Latino America Curaçao (VLAC) 2022 took place. A large sailing event, comparable to SAIL Amsterdam. CZMCARIB was closely involved in the preparations and was represented during the event with a defense village where Defense presented itself, including Caribbean military personnel and the Company in the West (CidW). Zr.Ms. Dolfijn and Zr.Ms. Pelikaan also made their presence known. International Drug Enforcement In addition to the external defense of six islands of the Kingdom of the Netherlands in the Caribbean, Defense plays an important role in upholding the international rule of law in the Caribbean region. Given the location of the islands, this primarily involves combating international drug trafficking by sea. The navy is thus closely integrated into the international drug enforcement organization Joint Interagency Task Force South in Key West. The Commander (kltz) of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean is therefore the commander of Taskgroup 4.4., one of the task groups of this organization.

Command of the Navy in the Caribbean SSCG was under the command of C-ZMCARIB. Until April, Zr.Ms. Friesland fulfilled this role, after which Zr.Ms. Groningen arrived as a relief in the same month. Zr.Ms. Holland relieved her in October. The SSCG did not have access to an NH90 this year. Therefore, for the duration of two rotations, the collaboration established in 2014 with the United States Coast Guard's Helicopter Interdiction Tactical Squadron continued. During these rotations, an MH-65 helicopter was embarked on board. In addition to the regular cooperation with the Dash-8 of the Caribbean Coast Guard, the SSCG had air support from the Dutch MQ-9 of 306 Squadron of CLSK this year. This improved aerial coverage was experienced by the SSCG as a force multiplier and a good step towards more intensive cooperation with the Air Force. Counter Drugs All three ships were deployed under both the flag of KW CARIB and for CTG 4.4 and were very successful during these periods. In cooperation with international units, CTG 4.4 and KWCARIB seized approximately 19,500 kg and 14,200 kg of contraband from the trade market respectively this year. Thus, 2022 is a record year. These international operations were conducted by KWCARIB in coordination with various countries including the United States, France, Colombia, and the United Kingdom in the US-led collaborative framework Joint Interagency Task Force South. Salute shots were fired upon the arrival of Zr.Ms. Friesland in Aruba.

Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean Cooperation with Defense The structural cooperation with Defense is described in a covenant between the CZSK and the Coast Guard. The covenant outlines mutual support in the form of personnel, resources, and services, and implements the management task by Defense and the execution by the Coast Guard, as established in the National Coast Guard Act. In 2022, this was also put into practice, and the cooperation was positive. The SSCG was available to the Coast Guard in 2022, in accordance with the operational availability of the ship. Command of the Naval Forces in the Caribbean Coast Guard Caribbean Director Coast Guard: Brigadier General (briggenmarns) F.O. Boots Deputy Director Coast Guard: E.H.G. Middelhof MBA The environment in which the Coast Guard operated in the Caribbean this year partly determined the priorities and deployment of its capabilities. Several factors underpinned the physically delivered output by the units and the results achieved. Venezuela Due to the unstable situation in Venezuela, the Coast Guard also monitored developments in that country in 2022. At the end of the year, discussions were set to begin regarding the reopening of the borders between Venezuela and the Windward Islands. Initially, this would concern the maritime borders for the transport of goods such as food. However, the discussions did not take place. In 2022, the Coast Guard saw an increase in the number of undocumented individuals from Venezuela; this year, 170 persons attempted to enter the islands illegally. Drug Smuggling The Coast Guard made several significant drug seizures in 2022, either in collaboration with Defense or third parties, intercepting 29,274 kg of cocaine and 5,116 kg of marijuana and hemp. Several chain partners with whom intensive cooperation took place in 2022 included CTG 4.4, SSCG, USCG, and the American Joint Inter Agency Task Force-South. Cooperation in 2022 varied from initial detection by flying units of the Coast Guard to joint operations and the use of the service's powers in international waters under the San José Treaty. Search and Rescue Cases In 2022, the Coast Guard rescued 598 persons from emergency situations. The service itself recorded 46 deceased and 11 missing persons in its area of responsibility. COVID-19 The Omicron wave of COVID-19 infections reached the Caribbean region in early 2022 and, like previous variants of the virus, also impacted the Coast Guard. This resulted in a temporarily reduced operational availability of operational units. Additionally, several planned initiatives for early 2022 could not be realized.

The Corps of cadets transforms 't Zaaltje and the surrounding areas into a richly decorated gala; each year with a different theme. The Corps of cadets works 24 hours a day in two shifts during this period to realize this theme. Originally, the Assaut was established by the Cadet Fencing Association Olympia as a fencing tournament, but it has since evolved into a three-day gala that returns annually. Page 11 11 FOREWORD Since 1488, we as a navy have provided security at sea and from the sea. We do this with fleet and marine units, supported by all those naval men and women on shore. And we do this with our national and international military and civilian partners. We do this far away and close to home. Since 1488, we have been at the center of history, adapting to new developments and learning from our experiences. By learning from history and the developments within it, we ensure that we remain future-proof, that we can effectively deter and fight to win. It is only logical that we document that history. The result of that logic can be found in this yearbook. I wish you much enjoyment in learning and reading. René P. Developments  
The CZSK (Royal Netherlands Navy Command) was in a difficult situation regarding personnel in 2023. Despite significant salary increases in 2022, particularly for sailors and corporals, the military branch still struggled to find enough new personnel to fill the growing organization. The civilian workforce did increase, which kept the total personnel count nearly stable. In 2023, to combat personnel shortages, the Defense Personnel Plan (DPP) and the Defense Component Personnel Plan (DOPP) were implemented. These aimed to significantly improve the personnel staffing of Defense. The DOPP included measures to increase intake, enhance personnel retention, accelerate career progression, and adjust the operations of CZSK. Some measures from the DOPP included:  
Introduction of the Service Year: on August 21, 2023, the first 12 service year military personnel began the First Maritime Military Training (EMMV). The service year personnel were assigned on board for a period of 9 months after the EMMV and basic training at the School for Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear Defense, Damage Control, and Operational Safety (SCBRNDC&BV).  
More focus on lateral entry and accelerating career progression. Various programs were developed to make officers and non-commissioned officers deployable more quickly. This includes accelerated programs for the sergeant Network Manager, sergeant Operational Service Operations (ODOPS) Weapon Controller, watch officer, and command center officer (CCO).  
More freedom of choice for future corporals after the corporal training. Implementation of the Marine Technician program, in which a partnership has been established with various Dutch maritime schools. Technical labor market allowance for certain groups of technical personnel.

The raison d'être of the DDS is thus the training of military divers. To fulfill this task, it comprises four formal training units and the 'informal' training unit T-squadron. Page 201 201 Appendices The availability of enforcement vessels at sea was lower than required for effective task execution. In consultation with the enforcement services and the Rijksrederij, the Coast Guard was able to deploy the emergency tug Guardian to fill some gaps in the sailing schedule. On the advice of the State Advocate, the planned assignment of ship crews from the Rijksrederij could not proceed, which meant that the patrol vessels Visarend and Zeearend were not deployable outside of the planned services. The additional sailing capacity for enforcement promised in 2023 is an absolute requirement to make a step towards 24/7 execution of this primary task at sea. In June 2023, the tender for the construction of the new Maritime Operations Center (MOC) and the Diversion, Testing, and Training Center (UTT) was put on the market, marking an important step in the realization of a new and modern Coast Guard center. This will have a positive effect on the operations of the Coast Guard. The preliminary award of the contract for the new construction has already taken place. Its delivery is scheduled for 2026. At the beginning of 2023, the Coast Guard did not implement the new incident management application, Guardion Coastguard, as planned. In particular, the market product purchased for incident registration, in accordance with the advice of the ICT Assessment Bureau, proved to have limitations regarding its usability in the operational center. The project replaced this component with a solution that is integrated into Guardion Coastguard, developed by JIVC Maritime IT. The Coast Guard reviewed its organization and mapped out the necessary personnel capacity that aligns with the assignments and ambitions of the clients from 2025. The required personnel capacity has been summarized in the Council for the Coast Guard in the so-called imbalance note. This also includes other necessary capacities, such as investments in personnel and ships to carry out 24/7 enforcement tasks and investments in personnel and systems for the execution of tasks in the field of Maritime Security, Enforcement, and Services. The Council definitively approved the resolution of this imbalance in June 2023 and allocated the necessary financial resources for this purpose. This allows the reorganization process to begin.
